## Credit Card Probability of Default {#sec-credit-card}

GP-based methods have been applied to credit-risk and credit-rating problems [@mahajan_gaussian_2022; @huang_using_2011], volatility forecasting [@munoz-gonzalez_laplace_2014], and market-risk approximation [@lehdili_performance-enhancing_2025], but direct DGP applications remain uncommon. Basel III makes banks' capital requirements explicitly risk-sensitive, so reliable probability of default (PD) estimates are critical for regulatory compliance [@basel_committee_basel_2011]. Under the IRB Advanced Approach, PD models must demonstrate high discriminative power (correctly ranking borrowers by risk) and accurate probability calibration (predicted default rates must track observed frequencies across rating grades) [@eba_gl_2017_16; @iasb_ifrs9_2014]. We therefore evaluate whether GP and DGP classifiers meet these regulatory criteria on a realistic credit-risk benchmark, and whether DGP depth adds discriminative value over single-layer GPs.

The benchmark is the UCI default of credit card clients dataset [@yeh_comparisons_2009], containing 30,000 observations and 23 predictor variables: credit limit, demographics, six months of repayment-status history, and corresponding billing and repayment amounts from April–September 2005. The target indicates default on the October 2005 payment. This benchmark is commonly used in existing credit-risk literature [@thomas_survey_2000].

#### Data Preparation and Experimental Design

Undocumented education and marriage codes were collapsed into an "other" category, skewed monetary variables (bill amounts and repayment amounts) were log-transformed to reduce leverage from extreme values, categorical variables were one-hot encoded with `drop_first=True`, and all continuous predictors were standardised to zero mean and unit variance, fit on the training split only to prevent leakage (see @sec-credit-risk-preprocessing-snippet for the implementation). The full 30,000-observation dataset was first split into a fixed held-out test set of 6,000 observations (20%), stratified by the target variable to ensure equal default rates across all splits.
The remaining 24,000 observations form the development pool. This ensures all models across sizes are evaluated on the same test set, giving a fair comparison across training-set sizes.

- Small: ($N_{\text{dev}} = 500$): 425 training, 75 validation observations.
- Medium: ($N_{\text{dev}} = 5{,}000$): 4,250 training, 750 validation observations.
- Large: ($N_{\text{dev}} = 24{,}000$): 20,400 training, 3,600 validation observations (full development set).

The validation split (15% of dev) serves two purposes: XGBoost early stopping and F1-optimal threshold selection for all models. Each model is first trained on the training set only and evaluated on the validation set to determine its optimal classification threshold $t^*$. All models are then retrained on the combined train+validation set and evaluated on the held-out test set using the validation-chosen threshold. The test set default rate is 22.1% across all tiers.

#### Model Set and Training Configuration {#sec-uci-models}

The model set and training protocol are consistent with @sec-kin8nm, adapted for binary classification with a Bernoulli likelihood. Three classical baselines are used: logistic regression (replacing Ridge regression from Kin8nm for the classification setting), random forest, and XGBoost. The same three GP-family models are used: SVGP, DSVGP-2L, and DSVGP-3L. All models are trained at each of the three training set sizes (small, medium, large) to characterise scaling behaviour.

#### Results at Full Scale (Large Tier) {#sec-uci-large}

| Model | ROC-AUC | F1 ($t^*$) | $t^*$ | ECE | Brier | Log Loss | Time (s) |
|:------|:-------:|:----------:|:-----:|:---:|:-----:|:--------:|:--------:|
| Logistic Regression | 0.739 | 0.500 | 0.50 | 0.225 | 0.199 | 0.590 | 0.03 |
| Random Forest | 0.769 | 0.532 | 0.35 | 0.087 | 0.146 | 0.460 | 4.85 |
| XGBoost | **0.779** | 0.536 | 0.50 | 0.196 | 0.177 | 0.539 | 0.24 |
| SVGP | 0.778 | **0.546** | 0.30 | **0.010** | **0.135** | **0.430** | 160.4 |
| DSVGP-2L | 0.777 | 0.540 | 0.30 | 0.014 | **0.135** | **0.430** | 197.0 |
| DSVGP-3L | 0.776 | 0.544 | 0.30 | 0.021 | 0.136 | 0.433 | 706.5 |

: Model comparison at full scale ($N_{\text{train}} = 20{,}400$, $N_{\text{test}} = 6{,}000$). Threshold $t^*$ selected on the validation set to maximise F1; all threshold-dependent metrics evaluated on the held-out test set at this fixed threshold. Bold entries indicate leading values. {#tbl-uci-large}

![ROC and precision-recall curves at full scale. XGBoost narrowly leads on ROC-AUC (0.779); GP-family models form the second group at 0.776–0.778.](/sections/4-modeling/assets/credit-card-default/large/roc_pr.png){#fig-uci-large-roc-pr}

![Reliability diagrams at full scale. GP-family models track the diagonal closely (ECE $\leq 0.021$); logistic regression and XGBoost show substantial miscalibration (ECE $> 0.19$).](/sections/4-modeling/assets/credit-card-default/large/calibration.png){#fig-uci-large-calibration}

XGBoost leads marginally on ROC-AUC (0.779), with the GP family following at 0.776–0.778, which a gap within the $\pm 0.015$ bootstrap CI, making the top four models statistically indistinguishable on ROC-AUC (@sec-appendix-uci-ci). At validation-chosen thresholds, performance converges with SVGP = 0.546 ($t^* = 0.30$), and XGBoost = 0.536 ($t^* = 0.50$). GP models' lower optimal thresholds (0.30 vs 0.35–0.50 for classical models) reflect narrower posterior score distributions which is a consequence of principled uncertainty quantification rather than a deficiency.

The standout result is probability calibration: GP models achieve ECE = 0.010–0.021 versus 0.087–0.225 for classical baselines, a 4–22$\times$ improvement requiring no post-hoc calibration [@niculescu_mizil_predicting_2005]. Under Basel IRB, PD estimates must track observed default rates across rating grades [@eba_gl_2017_16]; XGBoost's ECE of 0.196 suggests miscalibrated estimates that would likely require post-hoc recalibration (such as Platt scaling [@platt_probabilistic_1999] or isotonic regression). GP models' native calibration is far more consistent with these standards.

| Model | F1 (S), $t^*$ | F1 (M), $t^*$ | F1 (L), $t^*$ |
|:------|:-------------:|:--------------:|:--------------:|
| Logistic Regression | 0.475 (0.45) | 0.497 (0.55) | 0.500 (0.50) |
| Random Forest | **0.503** (0.40) | **0.530** (0.45) | 0.532 (0.35) |
| XGBoost | 0.477 (0.40) | 0.519 (0.55) | 0.536 (0.50) |
| SVGP | 0.501 (0.30) | 0.522 (0.35) | **0.546** (0.30) |
| DSVGP-2L | 0.498 (0.30) | **0.530** (0.30) | 0.540 (0.30) |
| DSVGP-3L | 0.362 (0.05) | 0.517 (0.35) | 0.544 (0.30) |

: F1 at validation-chosen threshold $t^*$ (shown in parentheses) across training tiers. GP models consistently require lower thresholds owing to their narrower posterior score distributions. {#tbl-uci-f1-scaling}

ROC and precision-recall curves and reliability diagrams at each training tier are provided in @sec-appendix-uci-scaling.

All models improve with more data, but the patterns differ by family. XGBoost shows the strongest discriminative scaling improvements (+0.045 ROC-AUC from small to large), while GP models converge toward XGBoost at large scale. DSVGP-3L collapses at small scale (ROC-AUC = 0.523, F1 = 0.362), a clear instance of the same small-data pathology observed on the Kin8nm dataset. Note that the anomalously low ECE = 0.005 for DSVGP-3L at small scale does not indicate good model performance as a model that consistently predicts near the base rate (~22.1% default probability) will appear well-calibrated by ECE despite its near-random discrimination.

On calibration, GP models maintain ECE $\leq 0.027$ from 425 training observations onward, while classical models are miscalibrated at all scales. XGBoost ECE actually worsens from 0.164 (small) to 0.196 (large) as more confident fits produce more extreme scores due to the lack of an intrinsic calibration mechanism [@niculescu_mizil_predicting_2005].

#### Computational Profile {#sec-uci-cost}

| Model | Time (s, small) | Time (s, medium) | Time (s, large) |
|:------|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|
| Logistic Regression | 0.003 | 0.01 | 0.03 |
| Random Forest | 0.43 | 1.42 | 4.85 |
| XGBoost | 0.02 | 0.08 | 0.24 |
| SVGP | 3.1 | 40.4 | 160.4 |
| DSVGP-2L | 3.9 | 46.5 | 197.0 |
| DSVGP-3L | 14.5 | 149.9 | 706.5 |

: Training time scaling across tiers. GP models scale approximately linearly with $N$; DSVGP-3L is $\sim 3.6\times$ the cost of DSVGP-2L at all scales. {#tbl-uci-runtime}

DSVGP-3L is the most expensive model at 707 seconds, approximately 3.6$\times$ the cost of the two-layer variant, yet gives no meaningful improvement over DSVGP-2L on any metric at large scale (ROC-AUC: 0.776 vs 0.777; ECE: 0.021 vs 0.014).

For deployment contexts, the GP training time penalty (197 s for DSVGP-2L vs 0.24 s for XGBoost at large scale) is a batch training cost incurred once per model refresh cycle. In credit-risk production environments where models are retrained monthly or quarterly, this is operationally irrelevant. Inference time for a single prediction is comparable across model families.

#### Summary {#sec-uci-discussion}

GP and DGP classifiers match XGBoost on discrimination (ROC-AUC within $\pm 0.003$, statistically indistinguishable) while providing 4–22$\times$ better native probability calibration - the property most important for regulatory PD estimation. This calibration advantage holds across all training set sizes, even from 425 observations. DSVGP-2L is the preferred deep configuration: it matches SVGP on all metrics (the 0.001 ROC-AUC difference is not significant), while DSVGP-3L adds ${\sim}3.6\times$ training cost with no measurable gain and fails catastrophically at small scale. The GP training time premium (${\sim}820\times$ vs XGBoost) is a batch cost incurred once per model refresh - operationally negligible in quarterly PD model cycles. The lack of DGP improvement over SVGP is consistent with @sec-kin8nm, confirming that the compositional flexibility of DGPs only yields gains on non-stationary target functions rather than the smooth credit-default surfaces typical of financial risk.
